Severe Flooding Hits Hong Kong Chemicals Plants, Disrupting Operations and Threatening Jobs

A wave of severe flooding following record rainfall in Hong Kong has caused significant disruptions to the city’s chemicals industry, with several major manufacturing sites and storage facilities reporting extensive water damage. The event, which began on Wednesday and intensified overnight, has led to halts in production at multiple plants concentrated in the New Territories and Tuen Mun industrial zones.

According to the Hong Kong Chemicals Manufacturers Association, at least seven large plants have suspended operations due to inundated processing units and compromised electrical systems. “Our members are facing unprecedented challenges,” said Association Chairwoman Linda Ho. “Safety protocols required immediate evacuation of staff and a full shutdown of key machinery, with floodwaters reaching up to 80 centimeters in some production floors.”

Early assessments indicate that losses in raw materials and finished chemical products could reach HKD 200 million. Storage tanks at several sites, including those operated by Kai Tak Polymers and Sun Fong Chemicals, have sustained damage, raising concerns about possible environmental hazards. Plant managers are currently working with emergency teams to contain leaks and prevent further contamination.

The floods have also affected thousands of workers in the industry, with union representatives warning of temporary layoffs and lost income. “Many of our members were unable to return to work today, and some fear they may not have jobs to come back to if the recovery takes too long,” said Lee Wai-chung, spokesperson for the Chemical Workers Union. “Safety remains our top priority, but there is real anxiety about the economic impact.”

Industry analysts expect ongoing disruptions as floodwaters have yet to recede and further heavy rain is forecast for the coming days. “The chemicals sector in Hong Kong is highly centralized, which amplifies the risks from such localized natural disasters,” noted analyst Eric Yuen of Pacifica Research. “Recovery will depend on how quickly operators can restore power, remove water, and restart production.”

Emergency response operations continue, with the situation still evolving at the time of writing.
